short: A pandemic carried home by troops from the Parthian war killed millions and strained the empire for a generation.
full:
Roman soldiers returning from Lucius Verus's Parthian campaign brought back a disease, likely smallpox, that spread through the empire from 165 CE and recurred in waves for roughly fifteen years. The physician Galen, who observed cases directly, left the fullest surviving clinical account, from which the plague sometimes takes its alternative name, the Plague of Galen. Mortality estimates vary widely, but the toll likely ran into the millions, striking army camps, cities and the imperial court alike; co-emperor Lucius Verus himself may have died of it in 169.

The plague thinned the legions at the same moment the Marcomanni and other peoples were pressing across the Danube, forcing Marcus Aurelius to conscript slaves, gladiators and provincials to keep the frontier armies at strength. Historians increasingly treat it as a hinge between the stability of the Antonine peace and the militarised, economically strained empire of the third century.
